title: Survivors of apartheid-era massacre are suing South Africa's government | CBC Radio
text:
Vincent Thamae remembers his grandfather telling stories about the Sharpeville massacre.

On March 21, 1960, South Africa's apartheid police opened fire on unarmed protesters in a township south of Johannesburg, killing dozens of men, women and children.

"My grandpa told me that those people who did that were not humans," Thamae, a Sharpeville resident, told As It Happens host Nil Köksal. "It's only when I grew up that I began to understand what he meant."

Thamae has been collecting testimonies from survivors and victims' families since 2018 for the organization Voices of Sharpeville. Now, he's a liaison between those survivors and a team of lawyers helping them launch a class-action lawsuit against the government.

The suit seeks compensation for victims and their descendants and calls on the government to strike down an apartheid-era law that shields South African officials from liability related to the massacre.

Thousands of people in Sharpeville were protesting apartheid pass laws, which restricted people's movement and enforced racial segregation, when police opened fire.

Police records from the time say 69 people were killed and 180 injured, while research cited by the plaintiffs puts the count at 91 dead and more than 238 wounded.

Abram Mofokeng, 87, was 20 when he was shot in the foot and back as he fled the gunfire. A bullet remains lodged in his back.

"It is not possible to forget what happened in 1960," Mofokeng said. "I cannot go a day without thinking about how we have been affected."

Mofokeng is one of three Sharpeville residents acting as representative plaintiffs for a wider group in the case brought by Lawyers for Human Rights.

The others, Paulina Mathinye and Ishmael Poho, both lost their fathers in the massacre when they were young children.

More than 70 survivors and relatives have expressed support for or interest in joining the litigation.

The government did not respond to requests for comment.

Those impacted have long been seeking compensation. In the aftermath of the massacre, around 258 claims were filed. But in 1961, the government enacted the Indemnity Act, shielding officials from legal liability and extinguishing the claims.

Apartheid officially ended in South Africa in 1994. But that shielding law remains in effect today.

Lawyers for the Sharpeville plaintiffs are calling for it to be struck down, arguing it violates their clients' constitutional right of access to the courts.

They also said the case seeks to address gaps left by the Truth and Reconciliation Commission process, under which only 51 Sharpeville survivors were formally awarded reparations.

Dan Leader, a partner at British human rights law firm Leigh Day, which is supporting the plaintiffs, called the case part of South Africa's "unfinished business."

"This is a time of reckoning for modern South Africa," Leader said.

If they succeed in overturning the Indemnity Act, the plaintiffs' claims for damages can proceed. The lawyers did not give a total figure for the claim but said it would vary for each claimant and would be worked out with the help of experts.

Thamae, a member of the Pan Africanist Congress political party, is hopeful that reparations could go beyond money and include more long-term benefits, like guaranteed access to education for the plaintiffs' children.

Many Sharpeville residents from that era, he says, were dispossessed of their lands by South Africa's apartheid government, the impact of which has reverberated through generations.

"They could not be part of the economy of the country," he said.

Thamae says collecting stories from survivors and victims' descendants has been slow and painful work that reopens old wounds that never fully healed.

"We still don't ... understand how other human beings can do the act that the government did to the people. We still haven't come to terms with what has happened."

With files from The Associated Press. Interview with Vincent Thamae produced by Kevin Robertson
